complexity.notes: The guard threshold uses n * bit_length(n) as a cheap stand-in for n log n, which is fine. Under the benchmark scaling (target = 2n+1) the counting branch is always taken, so it runs in O(n). One robustness issue: arrival times are compared as floats, so once target/speed grow past double precision the comparison can be wrong — comparing (target - p1) * s2 >= (target - p2) * s1 with cross-multiplied integers is exact at any magnitude. Minor style points: the AI-attribution comment is best removed, and the sort branch could iterate the sorted list in reverse instead of relying on pop() from the end.
complexity.summary: A guarded hybrid: if target is smaller than roughly n log n the cars are ordered by a counting array indexed by position, otherwise by a plain sort; then a single right-to-left sweep compares each car's arrival time against the current lead fleet's and counts a new fleet whenever a car arrives strictly later.

complexity.notes: Correct but exponentially slow; even n = 45 takes long. ||Memoizing the recursion (or iterating bottom-up keeping two running values)|| brings this to O(n) time, since ||each subproblem only needs to be solved once||.
complexity.summary: Plain recursive enumeration of the Fibonacci recurrence: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), with base cases at n = 0 and negative n. Every call branches twice with no caching, so overlapping subproblems are recomputed exponentially many times.

complexity.notes: Space can be reduced to O(1) since only ||the two most recent values|| are ever needed, and O(log n) time is achievable via ||fast doubling on the Fibonacci recurrence||. Under the unit-cost model this is O(n) time, but note the digit-level reality: F(n) has Θ(n) bits, so each addition really costs Θ(n) digit work — bit-level cost is O(n^2). The dict works but is overkill here; keys 0..n hash to consecutive slots so lookups are effectively collision-free, and a list would do the same job without hashing at all.
complexity.summary: Iterative bottom-up Fibonacci: seeds a dict with the base cases 0, 1, 2 and fills in each count up to n as the sum of the two previous counts.

complexity.correctness_reason: numpy's int64 overflows once n exceeds 92 (F(93) > 2^63), producing wrapped negative values as soon as the n <= 45 cap is lifted.
complexity.notes: The reported O(log n) is unit-cost arithmetic; the Fibonacci values have Θ(n) bits, so the true bit-level cost of the big multiplications is higher — worth knowing, though digit work is never folded into the reported figure. Pulling in numpy for a two-line recurrence is a heavy dependency, and it is also the source of the correctness issue: numpy uses fixed-width int64, so the result silently wraps once F(n) exceeds 2^63. A pure-Python version of the same matrix power (or any fast doubling) uses arbitrary-precision ints and would be correct for all n at the same unit-cost complexity.
complexity.summary: Computes the n-th Fibonacci number by raising the 2x2 transition matrix [[1,1],[1,0]] to the n-th power with numpy's binary-exponentiation matrix_power.

complexity.notes: Two performance issues, neither affecting correctness: pop(0) on a list costs O(queue length) per pop where collections.deque.popleft() is O(1), and nodes are only marked visited when dequeued, so a node is enqueued once per neighbor processed before it, letting the queue hold O(E) entries. On dense graphs this degrades the traversal to O(E^2) (Theta(n^4) in node count on a complete graph); adding nodes to a visited set at enqueue time restores O(V + E). The second pass building neighbor lists is clean and the empty-graph case is handled.
complexity.summary: BFS from the start node, creating a blank clone for each original node in a dict keyed by the original node (identity hash), then a second pass wires up each clone's neighbor list through the old-to-new map.

complexity.notes: Correct but does redundant work: the sort is unnecessary because the index-restricted recursion (each level only looks at nums[i:]) already prevents duplicate combinations, so `needs_sort` and the whole sorting step are dead weight; the extra public `needs_sort` parameter is also an awkward API wart. Each node pays O(n) for the `target in nums` scan, the nums[i:] slice copy, and the [nums[i]] + x concatenation; the standard idiom of passing a start index and mutating one shared path list with append/pop eliminates all of that copying without changing the algorithm. Space figure is recursion stack depth (t/min(nums)) excluding the output list, which is itself exponential.
complexity.summary: Recursive backtracking: sorts the array once, then for each starting index recurses on the suffix nums[i:] with target reduced by nums[i], prepending nums[i] to each returned combination. The `target in nums` membership test catches the single-element completion, and the target<=0 guard prunes overshoot.

complexity.notes: Dropping the previous version's sort loses nothing: the nums[i:] slicing already enforces a canonical order over combinations, so sorting was never load-bearing. Each call slices nums[i:] and builds [nums[i]] + x, adding O(n) and O(depth) copying per tree node; these are absorbed in the reported tree-size bound, though carrying a single path list with append/pop would avoid them. The `target in nums` check is a linear scan per call, likewise absorbed. Space quoted is for the recursion stack, where each frame retains its own slice; the output list itself can be exponentially large in t.
complexity.summary: Pure top-down recursion: for each index i, prepend nums[i] to every combination of nums[i:] summing to target - nums[i], plus a direct [target] hit when target appears in nums; recursing only over the suffix nums[i:] prevents duplicate combinations. In the bounds, n = len(nums), t = target, m = min(nums): the recursion tree has depth at most t/m and branching n, so its size is O(n^(t/m)), equivalently O(k * t/m) output-sensitive for k output combinations.

complexity.notes: Clean and idiomatic; seeding d[None] = None to avoid None checks is a nice touch. The dict keys are node objects, whose identity hashes the input cannot steer, so lookups stay O(1) even in the worst case. An O(1)-extra-space variant exists that ||interleaves each copy directly after its original node, sets random pointers via original.random.next, then unweaves the two lists||.
complexity.summary: Two-pass deep copy: first pass builds a dict mapping each original node to a fresh node with its value, second pass wires up next and random pointers through the map. The d[None] = None sentinel lets null pointers resolve through the same lookup without special-casing.

complexity.correctness_reason: A degenerate (fully skewed) tree of more than ~1000 nodes — well within the 100,000-node constraint — exceeds CPython's default recursion limit and raises RecursionError; the same traversal written iteratively with an explicit stack would not have this failure.
complexity.notes: Compact and idiomatic: using a default argument to thread the path maximum and adding the boolean comparison directly are both neat. The `else` after the early `return` is unnecessary. The one real problem is recursion depth — see correctness_reason.
complexity.summary: Recursive DFS that carries the maximum value seen so far on the root-to-node path via a default parameter, counting a node when its value is at least that running maximum. Each node is visited once; the recursion stack is O(h), which is O(n) for a skewed tree.

complexity.notes: Identical logic to the previous submission plus a recursion-limit bump so deep trees don't crash. The sentinel test `greatest == float('-inf')` to detect the top-level call is a bit hacky — setting the limit once at module level or wrapping the recursion in a helper would be cleaner. ||An iterative traversal with an explicit stack|| would sidestep the recursion limit entirely, though it has the same O(n) time and O(h) space.
complexity.summary: Recursive DFS carrying the maximum value seen so far; a node is counted as good when its value meets or exceeds that running max, and the sum over both subtrees is returned.

complexity.notes: The lands counter is dead code: it is computed and decremented but never read, since termination is driven by the row scan. Two things make this quadratic rather than linear: the linear membership test q not in queue on every neighbor check, and rescanning the grid from row 0 to locate each new island (up to O(n) scan work per island). ||Marking a cell as visited when it is enqueued, rather than when it is popped, removes the need for the membership test entirely and restores O(n).|| The border-padding rewrite is a neat way to avoid bounds checks, though it copies the whole grid; iterating neighbors with index arithmetic would avoid that.
complexity.summary: Pads the grid with a water border, then repeatedly scans rows for a remaining '1' and flood-fills that island with an explicit-stack DFS, zeroing cells as they are popped and counting one island per fill.

complexity.notes: A true O(n) solution exists: build the table once with ||the recurrence dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1), reusing an already-computed answer|| instead of re-counting each number from scratch. Also, on modern Python i.bit_count() is the idiomatic spelling of hammingWeight and removes the helper entirely.
complexity.summary: For each i in [0, n], counts set bits by repeatedly taking i % 2 and halving, so each number costs O(log n) bit-extraction steps and the whole table costs O(n log n). The O(n) space is the required output array itself; auxiliary space is O(1).

complexity.notes: Correct but slow: each edge removal calls prerequisites.remove([v, w]), an O(E) scan, and building the start list does an O(V) scan per prerequisite, so the whole run is O(E^2 + V*E). It also mutates the input list, which is avoidable. O(V + E) is achievable with ||Kahn's algorithm: an in-degree count array plus a queue of zero-in-degree courses, decrementing counts instead of scanning lists||. The dict keys are consecutive course labels, so hashing is not adversarially exploitable here.
complexity.summary: A reverse topological peel: it builds prerequisite and dependent adjacency lists, starts from courses that nothing depends on, and removes edges one at a time as each course's dependents are resolved, returning whether every edge was eliminated. The per-edge work uses linear list scans (prerequisites.remove, starts.remove, list membership), which makes it quadratic rather than linear.

complexity.notes: The algorithm is the right shape, but `p[1] in starts`, `starts.remove(...)`, and `parent[w].remove(v)` are linear scans, so the whole thing runs in O(n * m) instead of the O(n + m) this approach can reach; swapping them for ||a set for the zero-dependency courses and integer counts in place of the parent lists|| closes that gap. Otherwise clean, and dropping the O(m) `prerequisites.remove(...)` scan from the previous version was a good fix.
complexity.summary: A reverse Kahn's-style elimination: it builds prerequisite/dependent adjacency maps, starts from courses nothing depends on, and repeatedly removes a course from its prerequisites' dependent lists; if every entry gets removed there is no cycle.

complexity.notes: The algorithm intends sink-removal cycle detection, but as written it crashes (see correctness_reason). Even fixed, the start-list construction is quadratic because `starts` is a list; a set or boolean array would make that step linear. The standard linear solution is ||Kahn's algorithm: BFS from zero-indegree nodes with an indegree counter||, O(V + E).
complexity.summary: Builds a prerequisite list (child) and a dependent set (parent) per course, then repeatedly deletes courses that nothing depends on, removing them from their prerequisites' dependent sets; returns whether every course gets deleted. Building the start list with `in`/`remove` on a list costs O(numCourses * len(prerequisites)).

complexity.notes: Each element is pushed once and popped once, so the while loop is amortized O(1) per iteration — O(n) worst case, not O(n^2). Storing just the index on the stack and comparing temperatures[stack[-1]] would avoid the tuple unpacking and be slightly cleaner; the pair works fine as-is.
complexity.summary: Monotonic decreasing stack of (temperature, index) pairs: each new temperature pops all cooler pending days and records their wait, then pushes itself. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total work is linear even on adversarial inputs.

complexity.correctness_reason: A skewed tree deeper than CPython's recursion limit (~1000 frames) raises RecursionError, which the 100-node cap prevents but the generalized problem allows.
complexity.notes: Space is O(h) for the recursion stack: O(log n) on the balanced trees the benchmark generates, but O(n) on a skewed tree. Converting to an explicit-stack or level-order iteration would remove the recursion-depth failure mode at the cost of the same O(n) auxiliary space. The else after a return is unneeded but harmless.
complexity.summary: Plain recursive DFS: the depth of a node is 1 plus the max of its children's depths, with an empty tree returning 0. Every node is visited exactly once.

complexity.notes: word[1:] copies the remainder of the string at every recursion level, so strictly each level costs O(word length) rather than O(1); passing an index into a helper would avoid the copies. Dict keys are single characters from a fixed alphabet, so lookups are O(1) even adversarially. Recursion depth equals word length, which is fine at the stated cap of 25 but would need an iterative formulation for arbitrarily long words.
complexity.summary: A recursive trie: each WordDictionary node holds a dict of single-character children plus a terminal flag. addWord walks/creates one node per character; search follows the matching child and on '.' tries every child, so a dot-heavy pattern can explore the whole trie (n = total characters stored).

A minor style point: (pile + k - 1) // k avoids the float round-trip through math.ceil, which also stays exact for arbitrarily large pile sizes.

The chained pop() expressions are correct but dense; binding a, b (as done for '/') everywhere would read more clearly.

adversarial.note: n-1 distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, followed by a repeat of the last of them -- so a set-based scan does n-1 colliding inserts before it reaches the duplicate; the repeat itself is an exact-key hit, which CPython resolves by direct slot lookup, so the degradation comes entirely from the distinct colliding keys ahead of it

complexity.notes: Clean and idiomatic. Worst case is O(n^2) because the hashed ints are input-controlled (adversarial multiples of 2**61-1 collide), though average lookups stay O(1). The follow-up's O(1)-space target is reachable in O(n) time via ||Floyd's cycle detection, reading the array as a linked list where nums[i] is the next pointer|| — but that trick is only valid while values stay in [1, n]; it does not survive generalization.
complexity.summary: Single pass that adds each value to a seen-set and returns the first value already present. Under the scaling note the duplicate's second occurrence sits about two thirds of the way through on average, so the scan does a fixed fraction of the array.

adversarial.note: n-1 distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, followed by a repeat of the last of them -- so a set-based scan does n-1 colliding inserts before it reaches the duplicate; the repeat itself is an exact-key hit, which CPython resolves by direct slot lookup, so the degradation comes entirely from the distinct colliding keys ahead of it

complexity.notes: Correct but quadratic; your previous submission already solved this in O(n) time with a set at the cost of O(n) space. The follow-up asks for O(1) space and O(n) time, which is achievable by ||reading the array as a linked list (index -> nums[index]) and running Floyd's tortoise-and-hare cycle detection, since the value range 1..n makes the duplicate the entry point of a cycle|| — note that this trick relies on the value-range precondition, so it does not survive generalization, unlike your hash-set version.
complexity.summary: Brute-force all-pairs scan: for each index i, compare nums[i] against every later element and return the first value that matches a later one, which is the duplicate.

complexity.notes: The try/except-as-control-flow works but is convoluted: the sorted case is better handled by a plain range(len(nums) - 1) loop with a return of nums[0] after it, and a bare except is never good practice. Since the array is sorted apart from one break, the problem's stated challenge — O(log n) — is achievable with ||binary search: compare the middle element to the right end to decide which half contains the rotation point||.
complexity.summary: Scans left to right for the single position where an element exceeds its successor — that successor is the minimum. If the loop reaches the last index, an IndexError fires and a bare except returns nums[0], which covers the unrotated (fully sorted) case.

complexity.notes: The half-open-interval formulation with the descent test against the left endpoint is less common than comparing mid to the right endpoint, but it is correct and the (start+1) % len(nums) wrap cleanly handles the zero-rotation case. No correctness or complexity concerns.
complexity.summary: Binary search over a half-open [start, end) interval: comparing nums[start] to nums[mid] reveals which half contains the single descent, and the interval is halved until it pins the rotation point, with a modulo wrap to cover the unrotated case.

complexity.notes: Clean and idiomatic. The in-place mutation of the copied list is fine since nums is rebound to a new list. Space can be reduced to O(1) by keeping only ||the previous two DP values in rolling variables|| instead of the whole array.
complexity.summary: Classic one-dimensional DP: after prepending a zero, each position takes the max of robbing the current house (plus the best two back) or skipping it (best one back), so the last entry holds the answer.

complexity.notes: Both rob1's padded copy and the two slices make this O(n) space; O(1) is easy by tracking two rolling totals (prev, curr) instead of writing into a list. The len(nums) > 1 guard is needed since nums[1:] would be empty for a single house.

complexity.notes: The guard `s[i+length-1] in s[i:i+length]` is always true when length > 0 (a character is trivially inside the window that ends on it), so it only serves to skip the decrement at length 0; `length = max(0, length - 1)` says the same thing without the scan. complexity.notes: Correct and clear. Since each entry only reads the next two, the array could be replaced by two rolling variables for O(1) space, but the time complexity is already optimal.

complexity.notes: Compared to the previous version, this copies cost directly so the last two entries are already correct and the base-case assignments are dropped — a nice tidy-up. Space can be reduced from O(n) to O(1) since ||only the last two computed values are ever needed, so two rolling variables suffice instead of the full array||.

The recurrence is correct and the constant-space rolling state is already the optimal shape for this problem; no asymptotic improvement is possible since every cost must be read at least once.

complexity.notes: Correct and O(1) space, but each `in` check on a list is a full scan, making this quadratic. An O(n)-time, O(1)-space solution exists using ||the arithmetic-series sum n(n+1)/2 minus sum(nums), or XOR-ing all indices and values||; an O(n)-time alternative with O(n) space uses ||a set of the values for O(1) membership checks||.
complexity.summary: For each candidate value from 0 to n, linearly scans the list with `in` until the absent one is found.

complexity.notes: The set stores O(log n) values: after the first step the value is at most 81 times the digit count of n, i.e. O(log n), and it only shrinks from there, so the loop runs O(log n) iterations. The sq dict is fine but slightly redundant — int(d) ** 2 or a small tuple indexed by digit would spell the same thing without a ten-entry literal. There is a well-known O(1)-space alternative: ||Floyd's tortoise-and-hare cycle detection, advancing one pointer one step and the other two steps through the digit-square sequence||, which removes the set and the hash dependence entirely.
complexity.summary: Set-based cycle detection: repeatedly replace n with the sum of the squares of its digits (via a digit-to-square lookup dict) until it hits 1 or a value already seen. Each visited value is stored in a set, and a repeat proves a cycle not containing 1.

complexity.notes: Per-iteration cost is constant since the number halves each time. A faster variant, ||clearing the lowest set bit with n & (n - 1)||, iterates only once per set bit rather than once per bit position; Python's built-in int.bit_count() does this in one call.
complexity.summary: Repeatedly reads the lowest bit with n % 2 and shifts right via integer division, accumulating the count until n becomes 0. Runs one iteration per bit of the input's binary length.

complexity.notes: Correct and quite clever, but each of the n pops per permutation deletes from the middle of a list, which is O(n), so decoding costs O(n^2) per permutation rather than the O(n) a ||backtracking approach that builds each permutation by swapping elements in place|| achieves, making the total O(n^2 * n!) instead of O(n * n!). The recursion in `iterate` bottoms out with a `[-1]` sentinel that grows the returned list by one (harmless here since the loop just checks membership), and `place = 0` as a mutable-default-looking parameter is fine since it's only ever read. complexity.summary: Treats a length-n list as a mixed-radix counter (a factorial number system / Lehmer-style code), increments it n! times, and decodes each state into a permutation by popping the coded indices from a fresh copy of nums.

complexity.summary: Returns x**n in one line, delegating everything to Python's built-in exponentiation operator on floats.

complexity.notes: Stray print(a) debug line should be removed, and the loop variable i is unused (for _ in range(...) reads better). The true cost is Theta((log n)^2) multiplications — the benchmark model clamps this to n^0.5, the tightest expressible form. A faster O(log n) approach exists: ||standard binary exponentiation, squaring the base and halving the exponent in a single pass instead of recursing on the remainder||, because this version recomputes all lower squarings at every recursion level.
complexity.summary: Recursive exponentiation: squares x up to the largest power of two not exceeding n, then multiplies by the recursive result for the remaining exponent, handling negative n via the reciprocal. Each recursion level redoes its squarings from scratch, so the total number of multiplications is O((log n)^2).

complexity.notes: Compared to the previous submission this just drops a debug print and renames the loop variable. Each recursive level re-squares from scratch, so the total number of multiplications is (L-1)+(L-2)+... = O((log n)^2); ||a single loop that squares a running base while scanning the bits of n (classic binary exponentiation)|| needs only O(log n) multiplications. Turning the recursion into iteration would also cut the O(log n) call stack to O(1) space. The (log n)^2 runtime isn't representable in the benchmark grammar, so 'log n' is given as the nearest polylogarithmic form.
complexity.summary: Recursive exponentiation that peels off the highest set bit of n: it squares x repeatedly to build x^(2^k), then multiplies by the recursive result for the remaining exponent n - 2^k. Negative n is handled by recursing on 1/x with -n.

complexity.notes: Uses division, which solves the base problem but not the follow-up; ||a prefix-product pass followed by a suffix-product pass accumulated into the output|| would achieve O(n) without division and would also collapse the three-case branching into one uniform loop. The slices nums[:zero] and nums[zero+1:] each copy half the list — iterating over the original with index checks, or a single loop skipping zero, avoids the extra allocation. math.prod(nums) would tidy the total-product loop.
complexity.summary: Branches on the number of zeros: with 2+ zeros every output is 0; with exactly one, the product of the nonzero elements goes in the zero's slot; with none, it computes the total product and divides by each element.

complexity.notes: The `if size < 1` guard is dead code: the precondition guarantees at least one node, and an empty list would already be handled by returning prehead.next (None). A single-pass alternative achieving the same O(n) time with one traversal uses ||two pointers spaced n apart, so the trailing one lands on the node before the target when the leading one falls off the end||.
complexity.summary: Counts the list length in a first pass, then walks to the (size - n)th node behind a dummy pre-head and splices out the target. Correct two-pass approach with a dummy node handling the head-removal case.

complexity.notes: Correct for both parities; the termination logic (a+1 < b vs else-break, plus the a == b cleanup) is a bit fiddly — a cleaner loop condition could avoid the break, but this is just style. The O(n) extra array can be eliminated entirely: ||find the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half in place, then interleave the two halves|| achieves O(1) space with the same O(n) time. The `if not head` guard is dead code under the stated constraints (length >= 1) but harmless.
complexity.summary: Collects all nodes into an array, then walks two indices from both ends, rewiring each front node to point at its mirrored back node and the back node at the next front node until the pointers meet. Handles odd and even lengths with separate termination cases.

complexity.notes: Correct but more convoluted than needed: the base-case check, peeling off the head, and the post-loop fixup all disappear with the standard prev/curr loop that initializes prev to None and runs the rewiring inside the while body. That rewrite is purely cosmetic, same O(n) time and O(1) space.
complexity.summary: Iterative in-place reversal: walks the list once, rewiring each node's next pointer to its predecessor and returning the final node as the new head.

complexity.notes: Correct but uses O(n) extra space for the array; your previous submission solved the same problem in O(1) space by reversing the pointers in place, which is the approach interviewers usually expect here. The loop is a bit indirect: it appends a trailing None purely so `nodes[i-1]` reads None at i=0 via negative indexing — walking a `curr` pointer and appending until it becomes None would be clearer. The `for` loop also re-assigns `head.next = None` through that trick rather than stating it explicitly, which makes the termination invariant harder to see.
complexity.summary: Collects all nodes into an array (with a trailing None sentinel), then walks the array rewiring each node's next pointer to its predecessor, returning the former tail as the new head.

complexity.notes: Clean and idiomatic one-liner; the format spec handles the leading-zero padding that makes bit reversal nontrivial in string form. A bit-by-bit loop would have the same O(n) cost in the bit-width n; for a fixed width like 32, ||a divide-and-conquer swap that exchanges adjacent bits, then pairs, nibbles, bytes, and halves|| cuts the operation count to O(log n).
complexity.summary: Formats n as a zero-padded 32-bit binary string, reverses the string with slicing, and parses it back with int(..., 2).

complexity.notes: The whole strint class with its recursive __gt__ is over-engineered: the bound strings have a fixed 10-digit length, so the recursion and substring copying can never exceed that, but ||Python integers are arbitrary precision, so the 32-bit restriction can simply be ignored and the reversed value compared with a plain int comparison||, collapsing this to a few lines. Even staying with strings, ||direct lexicographic comparison of equal-length strings is built into Python||, so the recursive hand-rolled comparator is redundant.
complexity.summary: Wraps the input in a custom string-backed integer class, reverses the digit string, and lexicographically compares it against the string forms of the 2^31 bounds to decide whether to return 0 or the signed reversed value.

complexity.notes: The two branches for positive and negative x do essentially the same work and could be unified by splitting off the sign with abs(x) first. An ||arithmetic digit-extraction loop (repeatedly taking x % 10)|| is the classic alternative and has the same O(n) complexity here, so the string approach is fine.
complexity.summary: Converts x to a string, reverses the digit characters (slicing off the sign for negatives), and lexicographically compares the 10-digit result against the 32-bit bound strings to decide between the reversed value and 0.

complexity.notes: Flattening with sum(..., []) re-copies the accumulated prefix for every group, so the pass costs O(n^2/k) overall (worst at k=1); a single loop or itertools.chain.from_iterable would make this same array approach linear. The statement permits modifying only next pointers, but this rebuilds the list from copied values in freshly allocated nodes; ||reversing each group in place by rewiring pointers|| would respect that rule and drop the extra space to O(1). Minor style: iterate `for v in a` instead of range(0, len(a)).
complexity.summary: Copies all node values into a Python list, reverses each complete block of k via slicing, concatenates the blocks with sum(..., []), then builds a brand-new linked list from the result.

complexity.correctness_reason: A left- or right-skewed tree with more than roughly 1000 nodes (impossible under NeetCode's 100-node cap, but permitted once it is lifted) exceeds CPython's default recursion limit and raises RecursionError.
complexity.notes: Correct and readable. Stylistically, `not p and not q` is more idiomatic than `not (p or q)`, and comparing `p.val == q.val` before recursing would let unequal trees short-circuit slightly earlier. Space is O(h) recursion depth — O(log n) on balanced trees but O(n) on skewed ones, and because it recurses, a skewed tree deep enough to exceed Python's recursion limit would raise RecursionError; ||an iterative traversal with an explicit stack|| avoids that.
complexity.summary: Recursive simultaneous traversal of both trees: equal if both are None, unequal if exactly one is None, otherwise recurse on both children and compare values.

complexity.notes: divmod(n, row_length) is a tidier spelling of the index mapping. This already meets the O(log(m*n)) target.
complexity.summary: Treats the matrix as one sorted array of length m*n and runs a single binary search over virtual indices, mapping each index back to (row, col) via // and %.

complexity.notes: Idiomatic and meets the required O(n) time / O(1) space bounds. Python's arbitrary-precision ints mean negative values XOR-cancel correctly, so no special handling is needed.
complexity.summary: XOR-accumulates every element; pairs cancel out, leaving the unique element.

complexity.notes: Correct because the delimiter lies outside the 256-character ASCII set the problem guarantees, so it can never appear inside an input string. It would break under the statement's Unicode follow-up, where a ||length-prefix encoding (e.g. `len#string` per element)|| works for arbitrary characters without needing a forbidden delimiter. `output.pop(-1)` could be written more idiomatically as `s.split("😀")[:-1]`.
complexity.summary: Joins the strings with a non-ASCII emoji delimiter (plus a trailing delimiter) and splits on it to decode, popping the empty tail left by the trailing separator.

complexity.correctness_reason: Input strings may contain any of the 256 ASCII characters, so e.g. strs = ["paysutdlfmywvaugplk49w87ky9v478"] encodes to the delimiter concatenated with itself and decodes to three empty strings instead of the original.
complexity.notes: The delimiter swap is the whole story: the previous submission's 😀 sits outside the 256-character ASCII set the statement guarantees, so it can never collide with input content, whereas this ASCII-only delimiter can. ||Prefixing each string with its length|| avoids delimiters entirely and is the standard general answer (it also satisfies the follow-up for arbitrary character sets).
complexity.summary: Joins the strings with a fixed delimiter and appends a trailing delimiter, then decodes by splitting on it and dropping the empty tail. Both passes touch each character once, so total work is linear in the character volume, which here scales as n.

complexity.notes: The length-prefix scheme is the right generalization-safe choice, unlike a magic-delimiter join. However, decode re-slices `s = s[...:]` every iteration, copying the entire remaining string each time, which makes it quadratic in the total length; ||walking an integer cursor through the original string instead of re-slicing|| would make decode linear. Minor: the list comprehension inside join can be a generator expression, and the length parse could be a single `s.index('|')` plus slice without re-computing `int(s[0:a])` twice.
complexity.space: O(L), i.e. O(n) under the given scaling
complexity.summary: Encodes each string as `length|content` concatenated together (length-prefix framing), and decodes by reading the length up to the '|', slicing out that many characters, and repeating on the remainder. This is unambiguous for any content, including '|', digits, and empty strings.
complexity.time_average: O(n*L) where L is the total number of characters; O(n^2) under the given scaling since per-string length is bounded so L = Θ(n)
complexity.time_worst: O(n*L) where L is the total number of characters; O(n^2) under the given scaling

complexity.notes: Reading the bits with integer operations (i >> j) & 1 avoids the string formatting overhead, though the asymptotics are unchanged. Space is dominated by the output; auxiliary space is O(n).
complexity.summary: Iterates over all 2^n bitmasks, formats each index as an n-bit binary string, and collects the elements whose bit is set. This is optimal up to constants since the output itself contains n * 2^(n-1) values.

complexity.notes: Correct but very slow: `sorted(subset) not in result` scans up to 2^n stored subsets of length n for every one of the 2^n masks, pushing the real cost to O(n * 4^n) — the benchmark model field has no 4^n form, so 'n 2^n' there is the output-size bound, not the true runtime. Sorting each subset repeatedly is also wasted work. An O(n * 2^n) approach exists: ||sort nums once, then backtrack, skipping over duplicate values at the same recursion level so each distinct subset is generated exactly once||. Minor style point: f-string bit formatting works but `i >> j & 1` or itertools would be more idiomatic.
complexity.summary: Enumerates all 2^n bitmasks, builds each subset, and appends it only if its sorted form is not already in the result list, deduplicating via a linear membership scan.

complexity.notes: h is the main tree's height; a skewed generalized tree would hit CPython's recursion limit, an iterative or explicit-stack version avoids that. Worst case is quadratic because repeated values let the equality check run deep at every node; ||serializing both trees and searching for one in the other, or hashing each subtree bottom-up (Merkle-style)||, brings this down to O(n + m). The benchmark's distinct values make every non-matching check fail on its first comparison, so only the O(n) traversal is measured.
complexity.summary: Recursively walks the main tree and, at every node, runs a structural-equality check against subRoot, returning true on the first full match. The equality helper short-circuits on the first value or shape mismatch.

complexity.correctness_reason: The problem explicitly forbids the + operator, so `return a + b` violates the stated requirement on every input even though the numeric result is right.

A compliant solution would simulate addition with ||bitwise operations: XOR for the sum without carries, AND-plus-shift for the carry, looping until the carry is zero||, and in Python (which has arbitrary-precision ints) it would also need ||a fixed-width mask such as 32 bits with a sign correction|| to handle negative numbers.
complexity.summary: Returns a + b directly using the built-in addition operator.

complexity.notes: The unused 'import math' can be dropped. Like the previous a+b version, this sidesteps the problem's no-arithmetic-operator restriction rather than honoring its spirit; the intended exercise is ||adding bit by bit with XOR for the sum bits and AND-then-shift for the carry, looping until the carry is zero (with masking to emulate fixed-width two's complement)||.
complexity.summary: Returns sum([a, b]), letting the builtin sum perform the addition so the + operator never appears literally in the source.

complexity.notes: The dropped `import math` was dead code; good cleanup. sum() honors the letter of the constraint but not its spirit — the intended approach uses ||bitwise XOR for the carry-free sum and (a & b) << 1 for the carry, looping until the carry is zero||, which is O(1) for machine-width integers. Two-element list construction is fine, though sum((a, b)) avoids allocating a list.
complexity.summary: Sidesteps the operator ban by calling the built-in sum() on the two-element list [a, b].

complexity.correctness_reason: The hard-coded 32-bit width misinterprets any input outside the signed 32-bit range (e.g. a = 2**31 comes back negative), which the generalized problem permits even though NeetCode's ±1000 cap never reaches it.
complexity.notes: The numpy import is unused. The code literally uses the `-` operator (`d - 2**32`) and `sum(...)`, which the puzzle forbids — accepted because the judge can't check for it, but it defeats the exercise. The string round-trip (f-strings, int() per character, int(..., 2)) is a lot of machinery for what is one pass over bits; operating directly on the integers with ||bitwise XOR for the sum bits and AND-plus-shift for the carry, masked to 32 bits|| would express the same full-adder far more cheaply and without digit parsing.
complexity.summary: Converts both operands to fixed 32-bit binary strings, performs a manual full-adder pass from least to most significant bit, then reassembles the result and maps it back through two's-complement to recover the sign.

complexity.correctness_reason: The loop is hard-coded to 32 bits, so with the value caps lifted a = -2**31, b = 0 returns +2**31 instead of -2**31, and a = b = 2**31 returns 0 instead of 2**32.
complexity.notes: (a // 2**i) % 2 is a roundabout spelling of (a >> i) & 1, and 2**i is recomputed every iteration where a running mask shifted left would do. The len(range(...)) trick is O(1) (range length is computed arithmetically) but obscure. The sign test d > 2**31 is off by one — d == 2**31 should also be negative — though that input is outside the stated caps. The standard tidier form of this idea ||repeats a, b = a ^ b, (a & b) << 1 under a 32-bit mask until the carry is zero||, looping only as long as carries remain.
complexity.summary: Simulates a 32-bit ripple-carry adder: at each of 32 fixed positions, XOR of the operands' bits and the running carry gives the sum bit, a majority function propagates the carry, and the unsigned 32-bit result is mapped back to signed, using len(range(d, 2**32)) to compute the offset without the banned minus operator.

complexity.notes: The dedup-by-list-scan is the bottleneck: a dense input like [-k..k] produces O(n^2) distinct triplets, and each found triplet triggers an O(len(result)) membership scan, giving O(n^4) worst case. Checking membership against ||a set of the triplets found so far|| drops the scan to O(1) average, and a cleaner fix reaching O(n^2) total with no hashing is ||skipping over duplicate values when advancing low, mid, and high so each value-triplet is generated exactly once||. Appending tuples into the result is fine given the any-order contract, though the examples show lists. On the benchmark's distinct values, duplicates essentially never occur, so the scan is nearly free and measured time reflects the O(n^2) sweep.
complexity.summary: Sorts the array, then for each index low runs a two-pointer sweep on the suffix to find pairs summing to -nums[low]; each found triplet is appended only if it is not already in the result list, which is a linear scan of a list that can grow to O(n^2) triplets.

The O(n log n) sort is not optimal: an O(n) approach exists via ||bucket sort indexed by frequency||, which the generalized problem allows since counts lie in [1, n].

complexity.notes: Correct but quadratic: each call to max() rescans a slice, so the whole array is re-read for every position. The same idea becomes O(n) time (and O(n) or O(1) space) by computing the side maxima once — ||precompute prefix-max and suffix-max arrays, or walk in from both ends with two pointers tracking the running max on each side||. Stylistically, the one-liner with nested slicing and [0] padding is hard to read; a plain loop over indices with the two slice maxima would express the identical logic far more clearly.
complexity.summary: Brute-force: for every index, compute the min of the max height to its left and the max height to its right via fresh slices, subtract the bar height, and sum the positive contributions. Endpoints are forced to contribute 0 by padding the list with zeros.

complexity.notes: The inner repaint loop runs O(n) per level rise and there can be O(n) rises, giving O(n^2) worst case. An O(n) version exists that keeps the same two-pointer skeleton but ||accumulates the trapped water at each position as the pointer steps past it, using the running best level, instead of rewriting the whole window|| — that also drops the auxiliary array to O(1) space. Minor style points: `water = [0 for h in height]` ignores `h`, so `[0] * len(height)` is the idiomatic spelling, and `best = max(best, level)` makes the preceding `if level > best` condition the only place `best` matters, so the update could live inside that branch.
complexity.summary: Two pointers close in from both ends, tracking the highest water level seen so far; every time that level rises, the code repaints the whole active window with the new level, then finally sums the excess over each bar. The repaint-per-rise turns an otherwise linear scan into a quadratic one on inputs with many level increases (e.g. strictly increasing heights).

The index()/pop() reconstruction is convoluted and does up to three O(n) scans plus a mid-list pop; sorting (index, value) pairs with the original indices attached would let you read the answer off directly and drop the whole equal-values special case. Starting high at -1 relies on negative indexing, which works but is obscure. A faster O(n) average approach exists using ||a single pass with a hash map from value to index, checking whether target - x was already seen||.

complexity.notes: The sort is redundant since the input is guaranteed sorted (Timsort makes it O(n) here anyway), and the copied list breaks the problem's O(1) space requirement. Because the copy is identical to the original, the index-recovery scans and the pop branch are all unnecessary work: running the same two pointers directly on the original array would return the 1-indexed positions immediately, use O(1) extra space, and drop the four linear scans at the end. `List` is used without an import, which works on NeetCode's preamble but not standalone.
complexity.summary: Copies and re-sorts the array, runs a two-pointer scan inward from both ends until the pair summing to target is found, then recovers the original indices with list.index() calls, popping one element to disambiguate when both values are equal.

complexity.notes: Correct but unidiomatic: `valid *= isValidLine(...)` accumulates via integer multiplication and never short-circuits, so all 27 checks always run; `valid = valid and isValidLine(...)` (or `&=`) would be clearer and allow early exit. `line.count(num)` makes each line check quadratic in line length; a single pass with a ||set of seen values|| would be linear, though irrelevant at this fixed size. `List` is used without importing it from `typing`, which only works because LeetCode's environment pre-imports it. Amusingly, the deferred annotation rules of CPython 3.14 mean nothing here — these annotations are all fine anyway.
complexity.summary: Extracts each row, column (via list comprehension), and 3x3 box (via slicing), then validates each line by checking that no non-empty cell's count exceeds 1.

complexity.notes: The membership test `bracket in ["(", "{", "["]` is a fixed 3-element list scan, so it stays O(1) and there's no hashing involved anywhere. Style-wise, the repeated `elif` chain with `stack.pop()` inside the condition works but is a little awkward: it relies on `and` short-circuiting so the pop only happens for the matching close-bracket type, and the pop is repeated three times. A single pop per iteration (pop once, then compare, e.g. via a small dict mapping each close bracket to its opener) would be tidier without changing the algorithm. The empty input (excluded by the stated constraints but legal in the generalized problem) is handled correctly, returning True.
complexity.summary: Single pass pushing open brackets onto a stack and, for each close bracket, popping and checking that the popped opener matches its type; valid only if the stack ends empty.

complexity.notes: The dict is keyed by a fixed 3-character set, so lookups are O(1) worst case, not just average case. `bracket in "({["` is perfectly idiomatic for a tiny fixed alphabet. This is the same approach as the previous version, just with the elif chain collapsed into the lookup.
complexity.summary: Single pass with an explicit stack: push openers, and on a closer pop and compare against a fixed dict mapping closers to their openers. Valid iff every pop matches and the stack ends empty.
